title: Umm Salamah's advice
hookLine: at Hudaybiyyah the upset companions won't move, until on Umm Salamah's advice he shaves his own head first

cards: The treaty is signed. Nobody is celebrating. The companions came all this way in pilgrim white, and now they are going home without reaching the Ka'bah.

The terms feel like a loss to them. So when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stands up and tells them to slaughter their sacrifice animals and shave their heads, the sign that the pilgrimage is over, nobody moves.
He says it again. Still, no one stands. A leader, a crowd, and silence.

teach.b: The long report in Sahih al-Bukhari tells what happens next. He goes into his tent, to his wife Umm Salamah, who has traveled with him, and tells her what the people have done.
She doesn't scold them, and she doesn't tell him to give a speech. Her counsel is short and practical. Go out, she says.
Don't say a word to anyone.
Slaughter your own animal, and call your barber to shave your head. That's all. He does exactly that.
He walks out, speaks to no one, slaughters his animal, and sits for the barber. And the moment they see it, the companions get up.

They slaughter their animals and begin shaving one another's heads, the report says, so overcome with grief that they almost hurt one another. Some readers see it this way: the companions weren't defying him.
They were grieving, and perhaps still hoping. As long as he hadn't shaved, maybe the plan would change. Words couldn't end that hope gently.
His own shaved head could. Once he did it first, the question was closed, and they could follow. Notice also who saved the day.
Not a general, not a well-known speaker.
A wife in a tent, asked for her opinion and taken at her word.
Muslim teachers point to this scene when they talk about consulting family, and about how a hard instruction lands differently when the person giving it goes first.

how: Muslims retell the Hudaybiyyah story from Sahih al-Bukhari, and Umm Salamah's counsel is cited when teachers speak of consultation (shura), including with one's family.

o: the first woman to accept Islam in Mecca
the Prophet's wife whose counsel ended a standoff
the Prophet's daughter, who married Ali ibn Abi Talib

games.q: umm salamah's advice — tap the pairs.

s: the companions refused because they were defying him
the report says they were overcome with grief, and they rose the moment they saw him shave.
Umm Salamah advised him to say nothing and act
go out, speak to no one, slaughter your animal, and call your barber.
he answered their silence with a long speech
he followed her advice: he spoke to no one and shaved first.

games.q: you're the Prophet. you've told the people twice, and nobody moves. your wife says: what now?
o: go out, say nothing, and shave your own head first.
games.why: that was Umm Salamah's advice. he did it, and the moment they saw him, they got up and followed.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you keep asking other people to do, tidy up, put the phone down, show up on time, and notice how often it's been words.

Picture yourself simply doing it first, without announcing it, and think of one person whose counsel you could ask, the way he asked Umm Salamah. If you pray, you can ask Allah for the humility to go first.

wordCard.voice: Umm Salamah, the Prophet's wife whose quiet counsel, say nothing, and shave your own head first, ended the standoff at Hudaybiyyah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'mother of Salamah', the name she is known by; she is one of the Prophet's wives.

carryVoice: Your line: do it first. Sometimes the answer is an act, not a speech. That's day seven hundred eighty-seven.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731–2732 (Kitab al-Shurut, the treaty of Hudaybiyyah)
